probability-statistics-001.question: Three committee members are chosen from 8 people. If the members have no distinct roles, which of the following is the number of possible choices?
probability-statistics-001.explanation: Since the members have no distinct roles, the order of selection does not matter, so the number of combinations 8C3 is needed. 8C3 = (8 × 7 × 6) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 56. It can also be seen as the number of permutations 8P3 = 336, which distinguishes the order, divided by 3! = 6, the number of ways to order the same three people.
choiceNotes: This is the number of permutations 8P3 = 8 × 7 × 6, which distinguishes the order of selection. Because there are no distinct roles, it must be divided by the 6 ways of ordering the same three people.
This is 8³ = 512, which allows the same person to be chosen any number of times and also distinguishes the order.

probability-statistics-002.question: A chair, a vice-chair and a secretary are chosen, one each, from 5 people. If no one may hold two or more roles, which of the following is the number of possible choices?
probability-statistics-002.explanation: Because the roles differ, the number of permutations 5P3 is needed, which also distinguishes who is assigned to which role. There are 5 choices for the chair, 4 of the remaining people for the vice-chair and 3 of those still remaining for the secretary, so 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. Multiplying the number of combinations without roles, 5C3 = 10, by the 3! = 6 ways of assigning the roles to the three people also gives 60.
choiceNotes: This is the number of combinations 5C3, which ignores the roles. Even for the same three people, there are 6 different assignments of who takes which role.
This is 5³ = 125, which allows one person to hold several roles.

probability-statistics-003.question: A 4-digit PIN is made by arranging four of the digits 0 to 9. If the same digit may be used any number of times and the first digit may be 0, which of the following is the number of possible PINs?
probability-statistics-003.explanation: Each of the four positions can take any of the 10 digits 0 to 9, so the number of permutations with repetition is 10⁴ = 10,000. If the same digit could not be reused, there would be 10P4 = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5,040, and if in addition the order were ignored, 10C4 = 210. This number is also a measure of the effort of a brute-force attack that tries every PIN in turn.
choiceNotes: This is the number of combinations 10C4, without repeated digits and without regard to order. In a PIN, the order of the digits matters.
This is the number of permutations without repeated digits, 10P4 = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7. The question allows the same digit to be used any number of times.
Correct. Each position has 10 choices, so 10⁴ = 10,000.

probability-statistics-004.question: In a town whose streets form a square grid, you go from intersection A to intersection B, which is 4 blocks east and 3 blocks north of A, by a shortest route that moves only east or north. Which of the following is the number of routes?
probability-statistics-004.explanation: Every shortest route is a sequence of 7 moves: 4 one-block moves east and 3 one-block moves north. Choosing which 3 of the 7 moves go north fixes the route, so there are 7C3 = (7 × 6 × 5) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 35 routes. Calculating it as permutations with identical items, 7! ÷ (4! × 3!) = 35, gives the same result.
choiceNotes: Correct. The positions of the 3 northward moves are chosen from the 7 moves, so 7C3 = 35.
This is 2⁷ = 128, choosing east or north freely at each of the 7 moves, which ignores the condition of exactly 4 moves east and 3 moves north.
This is 7! = 5,040, which treats all 7 moves as distinct and ignores that swapping two east moves or two north moves gives the same route.

probability-statistics-005.question: Of 200 chips inspected, 30 had defect X and 20 had defect Y, and 8 of these had both X and Y. Which of the following is the number of chips with neither defect?
probability-statistics-005.explanation: By the inclusion-exclusion principle (number with X or Y = number with X + number with Y − number with both), 30 + 20 − 8 = 42 chips have X or Y. The chips with both are counted in both the 30 and the 20, so they are subtracted once. The number of chips with neither defect is 200 − 42 = 158.
choiceNotes: This is 200 − 30 − 20 − 8 = 142, which subtracts the 8 chips with both defects again instead of adding them back.
This is 200 − (30 + 20) = 150, which leaves the 8 chips with both defects counted twice.

probability-statistics-006.question: When a die is rolled 3 times, which of the following is closest to the probability that a 6 comes up at least once?
probability-statistics-006.explanation: The probability of "at least once" is easily found by subtracting from 1 the probability of its complement, "not even once". The probability of not rolling a 6 in one roll is 5/6, and the 3 rolls are independent, so the probability of no 6 at all is (5/6)³ = 125/216 ≈ 0.58. The required probability is therefore 1 − 125/216 = 91/216 ≈ 0.42.
choiceNotes: This adds 1/6 three times. It counts the cases with two or more 6s more than once, so the probabilities cannot simply be added like this.
(5/6)³ ≈ 0.58 is the probability that no 6 comes up at all.

probability-statistics-007.question: Among 10 lottery tickets, 3 are winners. Two tickets are drawn one after the other, and a drawn ticket is not put back. Which of the following is the probability that both are winners?
probability-statistics-007.explanation: The probability that the first ticket wins is 3/10. Given that the first ticket won, 2 of the remaining 9 tickets are winners, so the conditional probability that the second ticket wins is 2/9. The probability that both win is therefore 3/10 × 2/9 = 6/90 = 1/15. Thinking in combinations, dividing the 3C2 = 3 ways of choosing 2 of the 3 winners by the 10C2 = 45 ways of choosing 2 of the 10 tickets also gives 3/45 = 1/15.
choiceNotes: This counts only one pair of winners among the 45 ways of choosing 2 of the 10 tickets. There are 3 ways to choose 2 of the 3 winners.
This is (3/10)² = 9/100, the result when the drawn ticket is put back. Without putting it back, the probability that the second ticket wins changes to 2/9.

probability-statistics-008.question: A fab processed 500 wafers in a month, 100 of them in chamber 2. A total of 40 wafers failed, and 15 of these had been processed in chamber 2. Which of the following is the conditional probability that a wafer processed in chamber 2 fails?
probability-statistics-008.explanation: The conditional probability P(fail | chamber 2) treats only the wafers processed in chamber 2 as the whole and finds the fraction of them that failed: 15 ÷ 100 = 0.15. Written as a formula, P(fail | chamber 2) = P(fail and chamber 2) ÷ P(chamber 2) = (15/500) ÷ (100/500) = 0.15. It is a different value from P(chamber 2 | fail) = 15/40 = 0.375, with the condition and the outcome swapped, so care is needed about which one is asked for.
choiceNotes: 100 ÷ 500 = 0.20 is the probability that a wafer is processed in chamber 2.
15 ÷ 40 = 0.375 is the probability that a failed wafer was processed in chamber 2, with the condition and the outcome reversed.

probability-statistics-009.question: In a population of chips, 1% have a latent defect. A screening test judges 95% of the defective chips positive and wrongly judges 4% of the good chips positive. Which of the following is closest to the probability that a chip judged positive is actually defective?
probability-statistics-009.explanation: Considering 10,000 chips, 95 of the 100 defective chips test positive, and 396 of the 9,900 good chips also test positive. Of the 491 positives, only 95 are actually defective, so 95 ÷ 491 ≈ 0.19, or about 19%. Written with Bayes' theorem, P(defective | positive) = 0.01 × 0.95 ÷ (0.01 × 0.95 + 0.99 × 0.04) ≈ 0.19. When defects are rare, many good chips are mixed in with the positives even if the rate of wrongly judging them positive is small. This is called the effect of the base rate (prior probability).
choiceNotes: 0.01 × 0.95 + 0.99 × 0.04 = 0.0491 is the fraction of all chips judged positive.
95% is the probability that a defective chip is judged positive, P(positive | defective), which reverses the condition and the outcome of the required P(defective | positive).

probability-statistics-010.question: There are 1,000 lottery tickets at ¥50 each: one wins a ¥10,000 prize, ten win ¥1,000 prizes, and the rest win nothing. Which of the following is the expected value of the prize per ticket?
probability-statistics-010.explanation: The expected value is the sum of each value multiplied by the probability of that value. The probability of ¥10,000 is 1/1,000 and that of ¥1,000 is 10/1,000, so 10,000 × 1/1,000 + 1,000 × 10/1,000 = 10 + 10 = ¥20. Subtracting the ticket price of ¥50 gives an expected gain or loss of −¥30 per ticket.
choiceNotes: This is the expected gain or loss, the expected prize of ¥20 minus the ticket price of ¥50. The question asks for the expected value of the prize.
This is (10,000 + 1,000) ÷ 1,000 = 11, which ignores that there are ten ¥1,000 prizes.

probability-statistics-011.question: A chip costs ¥300 to make. A good chip sells for ¥500, and a defective chip cannot be sold and is discarded. If the probability that a chip is good is 80%, which of the following is the expected profit per chip made?
probability-statistics-011.explanation: The expected revenue is 500 × 0.8 + 0 × 0.2 = ¥400, and the manufacturing cost of ¥300 is incurred for both good and defective chips, so the expected profit is 400 − 300 = ¥100. Taking +¥200 for a good chip and −¥300 for a defective chip gives the same result: 200 × 0.8 + (−300) × 0.2 = 160 − 60 = ¥100.
choiceNotes: This is 0.8 × (500 − 300) = 160, which leaves out the ¥300 spent on making the defective chips.
500 − 300 = 200 is the profit on one good chip and ignores the 20% of defective chips.

probability-statistics-012.question: Ten keys are stored in a hash table with 100 buckets. Each key is assigned independently to one of the 100 buckets with equal probability. Which of the following is the expected number of pairs of keys that are assigned to the same bucket?
probability-statistics-012.explanation: There are 10C2 = 45 pairs of keys, and each pair lands in the same bucket with probability 1/100. By the linearity of expectation (the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values), the expected number of pairs in the same bucket is 45 × 1/100 = 0.45. Linearity of expectation holds even when the pairs are not independent, so the probabilities of the pairs can simply be added.
choiceNotes: This divides the number of keys, 10, by 100 and does not count the pairs of keys.
10 × 9 = 90 is the number of ordered pairs, which counts each pair twice.

probability-statistics-013.question: Taking the variance as the sum of the squared differences from the mean divided by the number of values, which of the following is the standard deviation of the 8 data values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9?
probability-statistics-013.explanation: The mean is (2 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 5 + 5 + 7 + 9) ÷ 8 = 40 ÷ 8 = 5. The squared differences from the mean are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32, so the variance is 32 ÷ 8 = 4. The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance, √4 = 2.
choiceNotes: Correct. The square root of the variance 4 gives a standard deviation of 2.
4 is the variance, the value before taking the square root.
5 is the mean of the data, not a measure of spread.

probability-statistics-014.question: Five products are taken from a process with a defect rate of 20%. Whether each product is defective is independent of the others. Which of the following is closest to the probability that exactly one of the five is defective?
probability-statistics-014.explanation: The number of defectives follows a binomial distribution with n = 5 and p = 0.2. The probability of exactly one defective is the 5C1 = 5 ways of choosing which of the five is defective multiplied by the probability 0.2 × 0.8⁴ = 0.08192 that this one is defective and the other four are good: 5 × 0.08192 = 0.4096 ≈ 0.41.
choiceNotes: 0.2 × 0.8⁴ ≈ 0.082 is the probability that one particular product is the only defective one. There are 5 possibilities for which one it is.
0.8⁵ ≈ 0.33 is the probability that all five are good.

probability-statistics-015.question: Inquiries to a service desk arrive at random, independently of one another, at an average of 3 per hour, and the number arriving in one hour follows a Poisson distribution. Taking e⁻³ ≈ 0.0498, which of the following is closest to the probability that exactly 2 arrive in a given hour?
probability-statistics-015.explanation: For a Poisson distribution with mean λ, the probability of k events is P(k) = λᵏ × e^(−λ) ÷ k!. With λ = 3 and k = 2, P(2) = 3² × e⁻³ ÷ 2 = 4.5 × 0.0498 ≈ 0.224. The Poisson distribution describes how many times a rare event occurs in a fixed time or area, and it is also used for the number of defects on a wafer.
choiceNotes: e⁻³ ≈ 0.050 is the probability that none arrive, P(0).
3 × e⁻³ ≈ 0.149 is the probability that exactly one arrives, P(1).
Correct. 3² × e⁻³ ÷ 2! ≈ 0.224.

probability-statistics-016.question: Requests reach a server as Poisson arrivals (independent, random arrivals) at an average of 6 per minute. Which of the following correctly combines the distribution followed by the intervals between arrivals and their mean?
probability-statistics-016.explanation: With Poisson arrivals, the intervals between arrivals follow an exponential distribution whose mean is 1/λ, the reciprocal of the arrival rate λ. With λ = 6 per minute, the mean interval is 1/6 minute = 10 seconds. The exponential distribution makes short intervals most likely, with a long gap now and then. The first M in the M/M/1 queueing model stands for arrivals of this kind.
choiceNotes: The intervals of Poisson arrivals do not follow a uniform distribution, and the mean mistakes the arrival rate of 6 for seconds.
Correct. The intervals follow an exponential distribution with a mean of 60 seconds ÷ 6 = 10 seconds.
The mean of 10 seconds is right, but the intervals of Poisson arrivals follow an exponential distribution, not a normal distribution spread symmetrically around the mean.

probability-statistics-017.question: The time to failure of a piece of equipment follows an exponential distribution with a mean of 1,000 hours. Take e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.61, e^(−1) ≈ 0.37 and e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.22. Given that the equipment has run for 500 hours without failure, which of the following is closest to the probability that it runs at least another 1,000 hours without failure?
probability-statistics-017.explanation: The exponential distribution is memoryless: the distribution of the remaining time does not depend on how much time has already passed. The probability of running at least another 1,000 hours after 500 hours is therefore the same as the probability that new equipment runs at least 1,000 hours, e^(−1) ≈ 0.37. Calculating it as a conditional probability also gives P(T > 1,500) ÷ P(T > 500) = e^(−1.5) ÷ e^(−0.5) = e^(−1). Parts in the random-failure period, where the failure rate is constant, therefore do not become more likely to fail the longer they have been used.
choiceNotes: e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.22 is the probability that new equipment runs at least 1,500 hours, which does not use the condition that it has already run 500 hours.
Correct. By memorylessness, e^(−1) ≈ 0.37.
e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.61 considers only the remaining 500 hours until a total of 1,000 hours, not the "another 1,000 hours" asked.

probability-statistics-018.question: You arrive at a bus stop served every 10 minutes at a random time, without checking the timetable. The waiting time follows a uniform distribution from 0 to 10 minutes. Which of the following correctly combines the expected waiting time and the probability that the wait is 3 minutes or less?
probability-statistics-018.explanation: In a uniform distribution every value in the interval is equally likely, so the expected value is the midpoint of the interval, (0 + 10) ÷ 2 = 5 minutes. The probability that the wait is 3 minutes or less is the fraction of the interval length, 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3.
choiceNotes: 0.7 is the probability that the wait is longer than 3 minutes.
10 minutes is the bus interval; the expected waiting time is half of it, 5 minutes.
Correct. The expected value is 5 minutes, and the probability of waiting 3 minutes or less is 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3.

probability-statistics-019.question: The dimension of a part follows a normal distribution with a mean of 50.0 mm and a standard deviation of 0.1 mm. Which of the following is closest to the fraction of parts whose dimension lies between 49.7 mm and 50.3 mm?
probability-statistics-019.explanation: 49.7 to 50.3 mm is the mean ±0.3 mm, that is, ±3 standard deviations (±3σ). For a normal distribution, about 68% lies within the mean ±1σ, about 95% within ±2σ and about 99.7% within ±3σ (the 68-95-99.7 rule). The fraction in this range is therefore about 99.7%.
choiceNotes: About 68% is the fraction within the mean ±1σ (49.9 to 50.1 mm).
About 95% is the fraction within the mean ±2σ (49.8 to 50.2 mm).
Correct. The range is ±3σ, so about 99.7%.

probability-statistics-020.question: A scored 80 on test X, and B scored 75 on test Y. Test X had a mean of 65 and a standard deviation of 10, and test Y had a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 6. Which of the following correctly compares their relative positions within their own tests using the standardized value z = (score − mean) ÷ standard deviation?
choices: A ranks higher, because A scored 5 points more than B
B ranks higher, because A's z is 1.5 and B's z is 2.5
They are at the same position, because both scored 15 points above the mean
probability-statistics-020.explanation: A's z = (80 − 65) ÷ 10 = 1.5, and B's z = (75 − 60) ÷ 6 = 2.5. Both are 15 points above the mean, but test Y has a smaller spread, so measured in units of the standard deviation, B is farther above the mean. Standardization makes it possible to compare relative positions even between data with different means and units.
choiceNotes: Scores on tests with different means and standard deviations cannot be compared directly.
Correct. z is 1.5 for A and 2.5 for B, so B is farther above the mean.
Both are 15 points above the mean, but the standard deviations differ, so their distance relative to the spread is different.

probability-statistics-021.question: The delay of a circuit path varies from chip to chip following a normal distribution with a mean of 940 ps and a standard deviation of 30 ps. Taking the fraction of a normal distribution within the mean ±2σ to be about 95.4%, which of the following is closest to the fraction of chips whose delay exceeds the clock period of 1,000 ps?
probability-statistics-021.explanation: Standardizing gives z = (1,000 − 940) ÷ 30 = 2, so the fraction of chips beyond the mean +2σ is needed. The fraction outside ±2σ is 100 − 95.4 = 4.6%, and since the normal distribution is symmetric, the upper side alone is 4.6 ÷ 2 = 2.3%. Treating the delay variation as a probability distribution in this way makes it possible to estimate the fraction of chips that fail timing.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the upper tail beyond z = 2, so (100 − 95.4) ÷ 2 = 2.3%.
4.6% is the fraction outside the mean ±2σ on both sides combined. Only the upper side, where the delay exceeds the period, is asked for.
95.4% is the fraction within the mean ±2σ.

probability-statistics-022.question: The response time of a server was measured 5 times, giving 20, 3, 5, 3 and 4 milliseconds in the order measured. Which of the following is the median of these data?
probability-statistics-022.explanation: The median is the middle value when the data are sorted by size. Sorted, the data are 3, 3, 4, 5, 20, so the median is the third value, 4 milliseconds. The mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7 milliseconds, pulled up by the single large value of 20 milliseconds. The median is a measure of central tendency that is little affected by such outliers, and the mode, the most frequent value, is 3 milliseconds.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the middle value of 3, 3, 4, 5, 20.
This is the middle value in the order measured. The median is found after sorting the data by size.
7 milliseconds is the mean, which is strongly affected by the outlier of 20 milliseconds.

probability-statistics-023.question: The 11 data values 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 20 are shown in a box plot. The first and third quartiles are taken as the medians of the lower and upper halves of the data, excluding the median. Which of the following is the interquartile range, which corresponds to the length of the box?
probability-statistics-023.explanation: The median is the sixth value, 8. The median of the lower half 1, 3, 4, 6, 7 is 4, the first quartile, and the median of the upper half 10, 12, 13, 15, 20 is 13, the third quartile, so the interquartile range is 13 − 4 = 9. A box plot draws a box from the first to the third quartile with a line at the median, showing where the middle half of the data lies. There are several conventions for computing quartiles, and the functions of spreadsheet software and the like may give slightly different values.
choiceNotes: 4.5 is the quartile deviation, half of the interquartile range.
Correct. 13 − 4 = 9.
20 − 1 = 19 is the difference between the maximum and minimum (the range), which for these data corresponds to the length between the ends of the whiskers.

probability-statistics-024.question: Which of the following correctly describes the correlation coefficient of two quantities?
choices: Even if the correlation coefficient is close to 0, there may be a curved relationship between the two quantities
When the correlation coefficient is −0.9, there is almost no relationship between the two quantities
The larger the correlation coefficient, the larger the slope of the regression line predicting one quantity from the other, without exception
probability-statistics-024.explanation: The correlation coefficient expresses the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantities as a value from −1 to 1. Close to 1, the points lie along a line rising to the right; close to −1, along a line falling to the right; close to 0, the linear relationship is weak. For example, for y = x² with x from −1 to 1, there is a strong valley-shaped relationship, yet the correlation coefficient can be close to 0. The slope of the regression line depends not only on the correlation coefficient but also on the ratio of the standard deviations of the two quantities.
choiceNotes: Correct. The correlation coefficient expresses only linear relationships, so it can miss curved ones.
−0.9 is a strong negative correlation, indicating a strong linear relationship in which one quantity decreases as the other increases.
The slope of the regression line is the correlation coefficient multiplied by the ratio of the standard deviations of the two quantities, so it is not determined by the correlation coefficient alone.

probability-statistics-025.question: Which of the following is closest to the correlation coefficient of the five data pairs (x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5)?
probability-statistics-025.explanation: The mean of x is 3 and the mean of y is 4. The sum of the products of the differences from the means is (−2) × (−2) + (−1) × 0 + 0 × 1 + 1 × 0 + 2 × 1 = 6, the sum of the squared differences of x from its mean is 10, and that of y is 6. The correlation coefficient is 6 ÷ √(10 × 6) = 6 ÷ √60 ≈ 0.77, a fairly strong positive correlation.
choiceNotes: This divides the covariance 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 by the product of the variances of x and y, 2 × 1.2. The correlation coefficient divides by the product of the standard deviations, which are square roots.
6 ÷ 10 = 0.6 is the slope of the regression line predicting y from x.

probability-statistics-026.question: Two quantities x and y have a correlation coefficient of 0.8, the standard deviation of x is 5, and the standard deviation of y is 10. Which of the following is the slope of the least-squares regression line predicting y from x?
probability-statistics-026.explanation: The slope of the regression line predicting y from x is the correlation coefficient × (standard deviation of y ÷ standard deviation of x), so 0.8 × 10 ÷ 5 = 1.6. This means that when x increases by 1, the predicted value of y increases by 1.6. The correlation coefficient does not depend on units, but the slope changes with the units and the spreads of x and y.
choiceNotes: This is 0.8 × 5 ÷ 10 = 0.4, with the ratio of the standard deviations inverted.
This takes the correlation coefficient itself as the slope. The slope equals the correlation coefficient only when the two standard deviations are equal.

probability-statistics-027.question: A sample of size 36 is drawn at random from a population with a standard deviation of 12. Which of the following is the standard error of the sample mean (the standard deviation that describes the spread of the sample mean)?
probability-statistics-027.explanation: The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n, the population standard deviation σ divided by the square root of the sample size n: 12 ÷ √36 = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. With a sample four times as large, 144, the standard error halves to 1, so doubling the precision of the estimate requires four times as many samples.
choiceNotes: Correct. 12 ÷ √36 = 2.
σ² ÷ n = 144 ÷ 36 = 4 is the variance of the sample mean, without taking the square root.
12 is the standard deviation of the individual values in the population; the spread of the sample mean is smaller than this.

probability-statistics-028.question: Which of the following correctly describes the meaning of a 95% confidence interval for the population mean obtained from a sample?
choices: It means that about 95% of the individual values in the population lie within the interval
If samples were drawn again and intervals computed by the same method many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the population mean
The larger the sample, the more variation it contains, so the interval at the same confidence level becomes wider
probability-statistics-028.explanation: A confidence interval estimates an unknown value, such as the population mean, from a sample with a range. A 95% confidence interval is an interval made by a method such that, if sampling were repeated, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population mean. The width of the interval is proportional to the standard error σ/√n, so it narrows as the sample grows.
choiceNotes: It shows the range of the estimate of the population mean, not the spread of individual values. The range containing about 95% of the individual values is the mean ±about 2σ, which is much wider.
Correct. It expresses that the method of making the interval contains the population mean about 95% of the time when repeated.
The width of the interval is proportional to σ/√n, so it narrows as the sample grows.

probability-statistics-029.question: The standard deviation of a population is known to be 10. A sample of size 100 drawn from it has a sample mean of 50.0. Taking the two-sided 95% value of the standard normal distribution to be 1.96, which of the following is the 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
probability-statistics-029.explanation: The standard error of the sample mean is 10 ÷ √100 = 1. The 95% confidence interval is "sample mean ± 1.96 × standard error", so 50.0 ± 1.96, which is 48.04 to 51.96. With a sample four times as large, 400, the half-width of the interval narrows to 1.96 × 10 ÷ 20 = 0.98.
choiceNotes: This is 50.0 ± 1.96 × 10, without dividing the standard deviation by √n. It is a rough range containing about 95% of the individual values.
This is 50.0 ± 1.96 × 10/100, dividing the standard deviation by n instead of √n.

probability-statistics-030.question: Which of the following correctly describes the meaning of the p-value obtained in a hypothesis test?
choices: The probability, calculated from the observed data, that the null hypothesis itself is true
If the p-value is 0.03, the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true is 97%
The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed result or a more extreme one
probability-statistics-030.explanation: A hypothesis test sets up a null hypothesis such as "there is no difference" and uses the p-value to express how unlikely a result like the actual data would be if it were true. If the p-value is smaller than a significance level decided in advance (for example 0.05), the null hypothesis is rejected and a difference is judged to exist. The p-value is not the probability that the null or the alternative hypothesis itself is true.
choiceNotes: The p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Subtracting the p-value from 1 does not give the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
Correct. It is the probability, under the null hypothesis, of a result equal to or more extreme than the one observed.

probability-statistics-031.question: Whether a product lot meets its specification is tested using a sample taken from it. If the null hypothesis is "this lot meets the specification", which of the following is a type I error?
choices: Judging a lot that meets the specification as not meeting it and rejecting it
Judging a lot that does not meet the specification as meeting it and accepting it
The instrument measuring the samples is broken, so the measured values themselves are wrong
probability-statistics-031.explanation: A type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, here rejecting a good lot (producer's risk). Its probability is the significance level α, decided in advance as 5% or similar. A type II error is failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false, here accepting a bad lot (consumer's risk). For the same sample size, making α smaller makes type II errors more likely.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the error of rejecting a true null hypothesis, and its probability is the significance level α.
This is a type II error, failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
This is a measurement error, not a type of error in the judgment of a test.

probability-statistics-032.question: Requests arrive at a service window at an average of 12 per hour, and each takes an average of 4 minutes to handle. Treating it as an M/M/1 queue, which of the following is the utilization of the window?
probability-statistics-032.explanation: The utilization ρ is the product of the arrival rate λ and the average service time Ts, and it expresses the fraction of time the window is busy. With matching units, 4 minutes = 1/15 hour, so ρ = 12 × 1/15 = 0.8. Using the service rate μ = 15 per hour, ρ = λ/μ = 12/15 gives the same result.
choiceNotes: Correct. 12 per hour × 4 minutes ÷ 60 minutes = 0.8.
This is 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25, with the numerator and denominator of λ/μ reversed. If the utilization were 1 or more, the queue would grow without limit.
This is 12 ÷ 4 = 3, calculated without matching the time units.

probability-statistics-033.question: Requests arrive at a server at an average of 3 per minute, and each takes an average of 15 seconds to process. Treating the server as an M/M/1 queue, which of the following is the average time from the arrival of a request until its processing is finished (the average response time)?
probability-statistics-033.explanation: The utilization is ρ = 3 per minute × 15 seconds ÷ 60 seconds = 0.75. The average waiting time is Wq = ρ/(1 − ρ) × Ts = 0.75/0.25 × 15 = 45 seconds, and adding the processing time of 15 seconds gives an average response time of 45 + 15 = 60 seconds. Ts/(1 − ρ) = 15/0.25 = 60 seconds gives the same result.
choiceNotes: This is 15 ÷ 0.75 = 20, dividing by ρ instead of 1 − ρ.
45 seconds is only the time spent waiting in the queue, Wq, without adding the 15-second processing time.
Correct. 45 + 15 = 60 seconds.

probability-statistics-034.question: A web server holds an average of 12 requests, counting those being processed and those waiting. Requests arrive at 40 per second and are processed at the same rate (steady state). Which of the following is the average time a request spends in the server, found from Little's law?
probability-statistics-034.explanation: Rearranging Little's law L = λW (average number in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system) gives W = L ÷ λ. W = 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 seconds. Little's law holds in a stable steady state regardless of the distributions of arrivals and service times.
choiceNotes: Correct. 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 seconds.
This is 40 ÷ 12 ≈ 3.3, dividing the wrong way round.
This is 12 × 40 = 480, calculating L × λ instead of L ÷ λ.

probability-statistics-035.question: For a server that can be treated as an M/M/1 queue, the arrival rate increased with the average service time unchanged, and the utilization rose from 0.8 to 0.9. By what factor did the average waiting time Wq (the time spent waiting in the queue) change? Which of the following is closest?
probability-statistics-035.explanation: Wq = ρ/(1 − ρ) × Ts, and Ts is unchanged, so the ratio of ρ/(1 − ρ) is needed. At ρ = 0.8 it is 0.8/0.2 = 4, and at ρ = 0.9 it is 0.9/0.1 = 9, so the factor is 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25. As the utilization approaches 1, 1 − ρ approaches 0, so a small increase in utilization makes the waiting time grow sharply.
choiceNotes: This is 0.9 ÷ 0.8 = 1.125, assuming the waiting time is proportional to the utilization.
This is the ratio of the average response time W = Ts/(1 − ρ), 0.2 ÷ 0.1 = 2, not the ratio of the waiting time, which excludes the processing time.

probability-statistics-036.question: There are two service windows of the same speed. In scheme A, each customer picks one of the windows with equal probability on arrival and joins that window's own queue. In scheme B, customers join a single queue and are served by whichever window becomes free first. Arrivals are random, and the total arrival rate and service speed are the same in both schemes. Which of the following correctly compares the average waiting time?
choices: Scheme A is shorter, because the queue is split in two and the arrival rate per queue is halved
Scheme B is shorter, because in scheme A one window can be idle while the other has a queue
They are the same, because with the same number and speed of windows the average waiting time does not depend on how the queue is formed
probability-statistics-036.explanation: Scheme A can be regarded as two M/M/1 queues side by side, each with half the arrival rate. Scheme B is an M/M/2 queue in which two windows share one queue, so a customer is served without waiting whenever either window is free. For example, with an average service time of 1 minute and a total arrival rate of 1 per minute (utilization 0.5), the average waiting time is 0.5/(1 − 0.5) × 1 = 1 minute in scheme A but about 0.33 minutes in scheme B. This is why a single queue shared by several windows is widely used, for example at the counters in banks and in server processing.
choiceNotes: The arrival rate per queue is halved, but each queue has only one window, so the utilization per window is the same as in scheme B. Moreover, customers in one queue cannot use the other window when it is free.
Correct. With a shared queue, a window is never idle while customers are waiting.
Even with the same number and speed of windows, the way the queue is formed changes the waiting time.

probability-statistics-037.question: A server with an average service time of 0.2 seconds is treated as an M/M/1 queue. To keep the average response time (waiting time plus processing time) at or below 1.0 second, which of the following is closest to the maximum arrival rate that can be accepted?
probability-statistics-037.explanation: The average response time is W = Ts/(1 − ρ), so 0.2/(1 − ρ) ≤ 1.0 gives 1 − ρ ≥ 0.2, that is, ρ ≤ 0.8. Since ρ = λ × Ts, λ ≤ 0.8 ÷ 0.2 = 4.0 per second. At an arrival rate of 5.0 per second, the utilization would be 1 and the queue would grow without limit.
choiceNotes: Correct. ρ ≤ 0.8, so λ ≤ 0.8 ÷ 0.2 = 4.0 per second.
This is the value when only the waiting time Wq is kept at or below 1.0 second (ρ ≤ 5/6, λ ≤ about 4.17 per second), which leaves out the 0.2-second processing time.
1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.0 is the arrival rate at which the utilization reaches 1, where the waiting time grows without limit.

probability-statistics-038.question: In an acceptance sampling inspection, 10 items are drawn at random from a large lot with a defect rate of 5%, and the lot is accepted if none of them is defective. Which of the following is closest to the probability that this lot is accepted?
probability-statistics-038.explanation: Because the lot is large, each of the 10 items drawn can be regarded as good independently with a probability of 95%. The probability that all 10 are good is 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.60. Even a lot with a 5% defect rate is accepted about 60% of the time, so the sample size and acceptance criterion are chosen according to which defect rates should be rejected and with what probability.
choiceNotes: 1 − 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.40 is the probability that one or more defectives are found and the lot is rejected.
This is 1 − 10 × 0.05 = 0.50, which simply adds the probabilities of finding a defective and so counts the cases with two or more defectives more than once.
Correct. 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.60.

probability-statistics-039.question: 10,000 bits of data are sent over a link with a bit error rate of 1 × 10⁻⁴. If the errors in each bit occur independently, which of the following is closest to the probability that at least one bit is in error?
probability-statistics-039.explanation: The probability that no bit is in error is (1 − 10⁻⁴)^10,000 ≈ e^(−1) ≈ 0.37, so the probability that at least one bit is in error is 1 − 0.37 = 0.63, or about 63%. When n × p is much smaller than 1, 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ can be approximated by n × p, but here n × p = 1, so this approximation cannot be used.
choiceNotes: 0.01% is the error rate per bit, not the probability that any of the 10,000 bits is in error.
This takes 10,000 × 10⁻⁴ = 1 as the probability, which counts the cases with two or more bit errors more than once. The n × p approximation can be used only when n × p is small enough.

probability-statistics-040.question: Eight data bits plus one even parity bit, 9 bits in total, are sent. If each bit is in error independently with a probability of 1%, which of the following is closest to the probability of an error that the parity check cannot detect?
probability-statistics-040.explanation: A parity check detects an odd number of bit errors, but an even number of bit errors leaves the number of 1s even or odd as before, so it cannot be detected. Almost all undetectable errors are 2-bit errors, whose probability is 9C2 × 0.01² × 0.99⁷ = 36 × 0.0001 × 0.932 ≈ 0.0034. The probability of errors in 4 or more bits is far smaller, so the total is still about 0.34%.
choiceNotes: 0.01² = 0.0001 is the probability that two particular bits are in error; it is not multiplied by the 36 ways of choosing 2 of the 9 bits.
1 − 0.99⁹ ≈ 8.6% is the probability of an error in at least one bit, which includes errors that parity can detect.
